questions.q: What is the explicit amount of money the narrator has for the rest of the month when he accepts the lunch invitation?
questions.a: The narrator explicitly states he has "eighty francs (gold francs) to last me the rest of the month." A wrong answer (e.g., "he has no money" or "he has 15 francs") reveals the student cannot distinguish between total budget (80 francs) and estimated lunch cost (15 francs), indicating poor literal detail retrieval.

questions.q: Explain in your own words the difference between a literal question and an inferential question using an example from "The Luncheon."
questions.a: A literal question asks for directly stated facts (e.g., "What did the lady order for lunch?" → salmon, caviar, asparagus, ice-cream, coffee, peach). An inferential question asks for implied meaning (e.g., "Why does the narrator say he will eat nothing for dinner?" → he has no money left after paying the bill). A wrong answer that gives a literal response for an inferential question (or vice versa) reveals the student cannot distinguish explicit vs. implicit meaning.

questions.q: The narrator thinks: "I would put my hand in my pocket and with a dramatic cry start up and say it had been picked." Apply the concept of dramatic irony to explain why this thought is ironic.
questions.a: Step 1: Identify the narrator's internal plan (pretend money was stolen). Step 2: Identify what the lady believes (he is a generous host). Step 3: The irony: the narrator's desperation contrasts with the lady's obliviousness; the reader knows his poverty while she assumes his comfort. A wrong answer that only describes the plan without contrasting perspectives shows the student cannot apply dramatic irony as an inferential lens.

questions.q: Analyze how the repeated phrase "I never eat more than one thing" functions differently each time the lady says it. What does this pattern reveal about her character?
questions.a: First instance: literal claim about habit. Second (after caviar): qualification ("Unless you have a little caviare"). Third (after asparagus): contradiction ("Just a bite... unless they had giant asparagus"). Fourth (at end): hypocrisy ("I was speaking for you"). The pattern reveals deliberate manipulation — she uses the phrase as a ritual to justify excess. A wrong answer that treats all instances as identical shows failure to track evolving subtext across the narrative.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the narrator's final statement — "Today she weighs twenty-one stone" — constitutes justified revenge or petty vindictiveness. Support your judgment with textual evidence.
questions.a: Justified revenge interpretation: The lady exploited his youth/politeness, impoverished him for a month, and showed zero awareness ("thought me mean"). Her obesity (21 stone = 133 kg) physically manifests her gluttony, validating his youthful suffering. Petty interpretation: He dwells on it for 20 years; "complacency" suggests moral smugness. A balanced evaluation weighs both. A one-sided answer without textual anchors (e.g., ignoring "I do not believe that I am a vindictive man") reveals evaluative bias over evidence-based reasoning.

questions.q: Create a new inferential question about the story that requires connecting the narrator's opening description of the lady ("more teeth... than necessary for any practical purpose") to the ending. Provide the answer with evidence.
questions.a: Question: "How does the narrator's initial physical description of the lady foreshadow the story's ending?" Answer: The "white, large, even teeth" suggest excessive consumption capacity; "more teeth than necessary" implies gluttony. This foreshadows her massive appetite at Foyot's and the final revelation of 21-stone weight. A weak answer that only describes her teeth without linking to appetite/ending shows inability to synthesize details across the narrative arc.
